newsitem.title: USA: U.S. magnesium prices flat as competition stiffens.
newsitem.headline: U.S. magnesium prices flat as competition stiffens.

text.p: Magnesium prices in the United States, the world's largest market for the light metal, remain flat as traders and producers jostle for business amid less tigher supplies, industry sources said.

Adding insult to financial injury, U.S. market players are trying confirm rumors that Russia's Solikamsk has gone over the heads of its traditional trader sales channels to sign a deal directly with General Motors to supply alloy magnesium.
General Motors and Solikamsk were unavailable for comment. If true, this would be the second foreign company GM has signed a supply deal with for alloy - Norway's Norsk Hydro was the first.
"The market is fairly static, but we are starting to see more inquiries - volumes have picked up dramatically," a trader said.
But another dealer added,"I have not had as many inquiries as I had hoped."
Spot market pure magnesium prices remain at $1.50 to $1.60 per pound, the lower end of the range for in-warehouse basis, the upper end for delivery to consumer's works.
Producers and traders are now battling each other to lock in sales for 1997 deliveries to consumers.
Pure magnesium is consumed in aluminum production and alloy is used to make diecast automobile parts.
Norsk Hydro's Hydro Magnesium division in Canada was said to be pushing hard to win a bigger slice of the U.S. pure magnesium market after being locked out by prohibitive dumping duties in the past.
Robert VanFleteren, vice president of marketing at Dow Magnesium said the U.S. consumers were being "aggressively pursued by all producers and Norsk is no exception."

"We are seeing a stepping up of activity by all the primary producers and all the traders. The market tightness that we all lived through in 1995 is not the same as the present condition...neither do we have grossly idled capacity," VanFleteren said.

Some traders believed many cosumers wanted a fixed price for the whole of 1997. "There are two ways you can look at that in two ways, either they want to know what their production costs are going to be, or they are worried about the price going higher," a trader said.
VanFleteren said there was no sign of a major consumer push to lock in prices for the whole of 1997 apart from some alloy buyers as the metal may not be consumed until some time in the future.
Stiffer competition is also likely to make it more difficult for U.S. producers to hike prices.
"One would have to look at the fundamentals to see if a price increase was justifiable, and you would probably get mixed opinion on that," VanFleteren said.
